Avoid plastic bottles and containers - your old kettle might even save you money over an electric kettle if you have a gas stove.

In most places, your tap water is of good quality. You can check every once in a while by fully evaporating a bottle of water, to see whether there's unusual stains. Salt and calcium are easy to recognise, all else is probably not a good sign.

Filters can fail, sometimes catastrophically - like when they get infested with bacteria or such, or leak unhealthy chemicals or metals. I suggest only using them if you have to filter anyways, due to the water quality in your region.

Distilling water is a sure way to get clean water, but you need to find a clean source of minerals (especially salt) to add. That is also true for especially good filters, like reverse osmosis. Also, distilling takes a lot of energy. If you have a lot of sunshine, you could get the energy for free by putting up a greenhouse over a pond, and collecting humidity. However, that requires some investment.

Rainwater I only suggest in areas where there are no bad pollutants in the next few hundred kilometers, especially towards where the rain usually comes from. All rain requires 'dirt' to condensate, which often comes from the exhausts of cars and the chimneys of factories. There's a theory that the wide-spread droughts in 1970s and 1980s northern Africa was caused by all the pollutants in Europe making the clouds rain off in Europe, while the cleaner air from the 1980s on allowed some recovery.

Most effective: stay informed about water quality, do as much as you can easily in your area (like checking your water quality with widely available testing kits) and punish brands which seem reckless in regards to water quality by not buying from them. Also, an aquarium and some knowing how a healthy fish looks can help you gauge water quality in your area.
